rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2 (Methodology) - the study reports its own documentary review of J<U+00FA>car basin water plans and allegations, a qualitative media analysis, and participatory action research (six meetings/workshops, Table 1) with ARJ, basin authority, regional government, city council and NGOs; Fig. 2 compiles ARJ gauging data 1980-2022.
rows.notes: The study does not measure irrigation water consumption under drip; its own results concern how planning instruments estimated and allocated hypothetical savings (1998 PHJ earmarked 240 hm3 of expected savings for new/re-endowed irrigable areas; 2015 PHJ deducted a theoretical 3037 m3/ha/yr saving from ARJ rights to compensate the Albufera wetland) and the stakeholder co-design of corrective measures. The authors' central argument is that drip savings are unproven 'paper water' subject to rebound effects. Fig. 2 (ARJ source data) shows conveyed water decreasing before modernisation and stabilising around 200 hm3 afterwards, and the text notes 40% less water used in the 2006-08 drought than in 1994-95 thanks to the new pipeline, but this is not presented as a measured reduction in consumption attributable to drip. The study does document that planning allocated expected savings to expansion of irrigated area, which touches the second half of the passage, but not as evidence that drip effectively reduced consumption.

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2 - own documentary review and participatory action research (meetings and workshops, Table 1).
rows.notes: The study reports no measurement or model of its own on groundwater recharge or groundwater levels. Section 3.2.1/Fig. 3 reports that public-institution technicians and NGOs in the workshops classified the decrease in surface return flows and the reduction in aquifer recharge as very negative effects of drip adoption, and section 3.1.3 notes that the 2015 basin plan admitted that savings were affecting aquifers; however, quantification of reduced return flows/infiltration is attributed to cited work (Ruiz-Rodr<U+00ED>guez 2017; Pool et al. 2021, 2022), and the effect on springs is stated as not yet quantified. The study's own contribution is a stakeholder diagnosis and documentary analysis, not evidence on the hydrological effect; the passage itself also concerns reduced consumption and expansion rather than recharge.

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2 - own documentary review and participatory action research.
rows.notes: The study contains nothing on plant height, harvest weight or crop yield under drip. The only production-related statement is a cited estimate (Ruiz-Rodr<U+00ED>guez et al., 2017) that drip adoption raises agricultural income by about 800 EUR/ha, reported in the workshop diagnosis. The citation in the passage may refer to a different Sanchis-Ibor et al. 2024 publication.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a governance/water-allocation case study (documentary analysis plus participatory action research) on the Acequia Real del J<U+00FA>car and the Albufera wetland; it does not report agronomic or hydrological measurements of its own, and its thesis is that drip water savings are unproven and subject to rebound effects.
